title: Perplexity launches a local AI agent with zero token costs
summary: All you need is a $5,000 NVIDIA setup.
body: TL;DR Perplexity has launched a new agentic AI tool called “Portable Computer” that runs locally on users’ devices. It uses small, efficient models such as Qwen 3.8 and NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning. It will not incur token costs for tasks completed locally, but can connect to cloud models if needed. Months after launching its agentic AI tool, “Personal Computer,” Perplexity is introducing a new option for users who prefer to run their AI agents locally . The company today announced “Portable Computer,” its local-first agent, in partnership with NVIDIA. Portable Computer will run entirely on-device. The agent, along with the models and other tools, lives locally on the user’s device. This ensures that user data isn’t sent to the cloud and offers a higher level of privacy for sensitive data.

title: Apps may keep giving us tools to break our addiction to them, but teens aren’t using them
summary: Guess how many teens use anti-doomscrolling features. Hint: It's NOT "practically everyone."
body: TL;DR Tools like Digital Wellbeing or Instagram’s Take a Break are built to interrupt addictive use cycles. In an ongoing Meta trial, a former data scientist shares just how few teens actually took advantage of the company’s tools. With teen accounts, Take a Break is now on by default, hopefully pushing numbers up a little. Are smartphones our best friends, or our worst enemies? Sometimes it feels like half the work companies are putting into new features are attempts to fix our addiction to others, like with the new Pause Point on Pixel 11 devices — or really anything Digital Wellbeing , for that matter. And while we seem to keep getting more and more new tools meant to save us from ourselves, are the most vulnerable people even using them? According to Meta, maybe not so much. Meta’s currently being sued by 29 states over claims of safety and privacy issues impacting its youngest users, and Bloomberg is sharing some of the details just revealed by a former Meta data scientist’s testimony.

title: Fan survey sends Google a pretty blunt message about the Pixel 12
summary: Our readers told us what the Pixel 12's focus should be, and it's not more AI.
body: Like it or not, Google has made AI a huge part of the Pixel experience, and that’s only become more obvious with the Pixel 11 series. Gemini Intelligence and other smart features were a major focus of this year’s launch — so much so that you’d assume this was what all the fans were screaming out for. It’s always quite tricky to know how true that is, so we were curious about where you think Google needs to go next with the Pixel 12. We recently asked our readers exactly that. My colleague Robert Trigg certainly has his own ideas about this direction, and made them abundantly clear in a recent article . His argument in a nutshell is that the Pixel 11 shows Google is approaching something of a hardware breaking point. He wasn’t unhappy with Google’s AI work, but pointed out that rival flagships are pushing ahead in fundamental areas such as battery capacity, charging speeds, camera hardware, and raw performance, while Pixels haven’t kept pace. With the Pixel 12 next to face that challenge, we asked you via a poll in the article whether Google should prioritize better hardware, even smarter AI, both, or simply more competitive prices.

title: Claude Cowork will now remember your conversations with chat

body: Credit: Stephen Radochia / Android Authority TL;DR Claude chat and Cowork now share the same memory. It has been about a week since Anthropic gave Claude the ability to send emails in Gmail and manage files in Google Drive. Now the AI company is rolling out another feature. This feature will make switching back and forth between Claude chat and Cowork a little easier. Anthropic has announced that Claude Cowork now has memory, so you can spend less time re-explaining. Not only does Cowork have memory, but it also shares the same memory as chat. That means when you run a task in Cowork, Claude will remember it in chat, and vice versa.

title: Google Home made users say the weirdest thing to set an alarm, but that’s over now
summary: It's a small fix, but a welcome one for anyone who relies on voice alarms daily.
body: TL;DR Some Google Home devices stopped setting alarms via voice command for several days. The bug hit both Google Assistant and Gemini for Home, affecting Nest speakers, displays, and even third-party devices like Lenovo smart displays. Google has confirmed the fix, and our own testing shows alarms are setting and triggering correctly again. Google Home has had a busy August, with Google rolling out several updates that make Gemini for Home smarter and add new capabilities to its smart home platform. But amid all those improvements, something as basic as setting an alarm suddenly stopped working for some users. Thankfully, Google has now confirmed that the issue affecting Nest and other Gemini-powered smart home devices has been fixed. For several days, users on Reddit reported that commands such as “Hey Google, set an alarm for 8:30 AM” would simply be ignored. Some found that alarms worked when set for an exact hour, while others had to ask Google to set an alarm first and then provide the time when prompted. One odd workaround involved saying “Hey Google, hi” before giving the alarm command.

title: The Pixel 11 Pro’s camera flash is a ‘LoLight’ thanks to HiLight
summary: Users complain that the Pixel 11 Pro's camera flash is a big downgrade over other phones, and HiLight could be to blame here.
body: Credit: Sanuj Bhatia / Android Authority TL;DR Reddit users report that the Google Pixel 11 Pro’s camera flash is significantly weaker than that of older Pixels and competitors. Our preliminary testing here at Android Authority shows the Pixel 11 Pro XL torch mode registered 89 lux compared to 123 lux on the Pixel 10 Pro XL. The physical diffuser added to the camera visor for the new HiLight LED array is likely the cause of the softer beam. Google’s new Pixel 11 Pro series introduces HiLight , a small array of ambient LEDs around the camera flash that give you some bits of information without requiring you to turn over or unlock your phone. Google ended up severely limiting HiLight’s functionality, and users had to resort to apps like HiLight Studio to unlock the LED’s full potential. As it turns out, Google gimped HiLight in more ways than one, with the LED flash itself also downgraded compared to the Pixel 10 series. Reddit user pcman2000 voiced their frustration with the Pixel 11 Pro’s camera flash, calling it “really weak” and the weakest among all the phones they tested, ranking it below the Pixel 9 Pro and even the iPhone 17e.

title: Forget iPhones — this hack brings Quick Share to Kindles
summary: An unofficial project called Kindshare adds Quick Share to jailbroken Kindles, with a few key limitations.
body: Credit: Kaitlyn Cimino / Android Authority TL;DR An unofficial project brings Quick Share receiving to jailbroken Kindle devices. Kindshare lets you send files wirelessly from an Android phone, but the Kindle can’t send files back. The process is fairly technical, and compatibility may depend on your Kindle model and firmware version. Quick Share made an unexpected leap beyond Android last year when Google made it compatible with Apple’s AirDrop . Now it’s more or less reached another device you probably wouldn’t have expected, as an unofficial project lets you send files from an Android phone straight to a jailbroken Kindle. As spotted by Hackaday , developer unrealJune has created Kindshare, an open-source project that adds Quick Share receiving to compatible Kindles. Once everything is set up, the Kindle can appear as a destination in Quick Share, letting you send files over wirelessly.

title: Google, take note: This phone maker’s new chipset looks like an absolute beast
summary: It even has an unannounced GPU.
body: TL;DR Xiaomi has announced the XRing 03 smartphone chipset. This chipset has an unannounced Arm G2-Ultra NX GPU and a 10-core CPU with no little cores. The chip will debut in the Xiaomi 18 Fold, which is scheduled to launch next month. Google has just launched the Pixel 11 series , and our own benchmarks show that the Tensor G6 chip is a significant step down from rival chips. Now, Xiaomi has revealed its XRing 03 processor, and it seemingly obliterates Google’s silicon on paper. Xiaomi revealed XRing 03 details on Weibo , and it packs a 3nm design from an unspecified foundry. However, what’s particularly interesting is that it comes with an unannounced Arm G2-Ultra NX GPU. Expect 16 cores, eight NX neural accelerators, and AI-based super-resolution/frame interpolation. In fact, Xiaomi claims that this GPU is 85% faster than last year’s XRing 01 , 64% more efficient, and 182% faster at ray tracing. For what it’s worth, the XRing 01 had an Immortalis G925 MC16 GPU. Either way, this seems far more impressive than the Tensor G6’s PowerVR CXTP-48-1536 GPU.

body: Credit: Megan Ellis / Android Authority The Play Store has no shortage of weather apps, but most of them are paywalled, ad-heavy, or just not that good. Breezy Weather is none of those things. It’s free, open-source, and one of the most feature-rich weather apps available for Android. But since you’re here, I’m guessing you already know all that. The real question is how to get Breezy Weather on your phone, as it’s not on the Play Store — and more importantly, how to keep it updated. There are a few ways to do it, and none of them are complicated.

title: Nintendo just went nuclear on Switch emulators (again)
summary: Nintendo just can't stand Switch games running on anything other than a Switch.
body: TL;DR Nintendo has filed seven new DMCA notices taking down over 400 GitHub repositories related to Switch emulators. The notice took down repos for emulators such as Suyu, Skyline, and several others. It’s no secret that Nintendo has historically taken an extremely strict stance against emulators and people using its IP without permission. A few months ago, the company sent DMCA notices to take down several Switch emulators whose code was hosted on GitHub. Now, the company has thrown another proverbial Donkey Kong barrel at more such GitHub repositories. Nintendo has filed seven DMCA complaints with GitHub to take down over 400 repositories related to Switch emulators in a single day (via TorrentFreak ). This includes emulators like Suyu, which gained popularity after the Yuzu emulator shut down in 2024. According to the DMCA notice displayed publicly on the Suyu repository, GitHub took down all 311 repositories in the network due to Nintendo’s DMCA notice.

title: Pixel 11 Pro Fold cracks in bend test despite Google’s ‘3x stronger’ claims
summary: This makes the Pixel 11 Pro Fold the fourth consecutive Google foldable to fail in this aspect.
body: Credit: Joe Maring / Android Authority TL;DR The Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold has failed JerryRigEverything’s popular bend test. The phone cracked along both antenna lines next to the hinge, and its outer display also popped right off during the test. Google has touted a redesigned build that is three times stronger, but it looks like the same antenna-line area is still the phone’s weakest point, and the battery placement is also not ideal. Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold has failed JerryRigEverything’s popular durability test for a second year in a row. After the Pixel 10 Pro XL literally exploded during the same durability test last year, it looks like Google still hasn’t improved the Pixel 11 Pro’s weakest structural point.

title: Google wants $1,099 for the Pixel 11 Pro — here’s how I paid only $399
summary: All those promos add up fast.
body: There’s a lot to talk about with Google’s Pixel 11 series, but something that keeps coming up is how expensive the phones are. As we’ve seen from virtually every tech company this year, each Pixel 11 model is more expensive than its predecessor. The starting price of every Pixel 11 phone is $100 higher than its Pixel 10 counterpart, and the Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL also have less RAM than before . It’s a crummy situation all around, and I wouldn’t blame you if hearing this has put you off from buying a Pixel 11 entirely.

title: Android Pulse app may already be on your phone, and now we know what it does
summary: Google gave Android a Pulse, and it's keeping tabs on trouble.
body: TL;DR Google’s Android Pulse app is starting to appear as an available update in the Play Store. The background service appears to detect unusual resource usage, such as apps suddenly consuming too much battery, memory, or processing power. Android Pulse isn’t new; builds date back to March, and the Play Store shows more than 10 million downloads. There are plenty of Google apps you probably use every day, but Android Pulse is definitely not one of them. In fact, you may not even know it exists. That could change soon, though, because this mysterious system app is suddenly showing up as an available update in the Play Store. As first spotted by 9to5Google , Android Pulse is a Google-made app that works behind the scenes. Its job appears to be pretty simple: keep an eye out for apps or parts of Android that are using your phone’s resources in unusual ways.
